Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Najm (The Star)

It is Meccan. According to some, however, the exception is the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾ to the end of the verse. He said: it was revealed in Medina.

This is the first surah which the Prophet (ﷺ) made public, and he recited it aloud before the polytheists.

As for the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿By the star﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, in a narration of al-Walibi, said it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), which is one of the two reports from Mujahid. Asbat narrated from al-Suddi that it is Venus (al-Zuhra). And from Ibn 'Abbas in another narration, and this is the view of a group, the intended meaning is the Qur'an, which was sent down star by star over twenty years. It was also said: over twenty-three years.

The fourth view: the view of Qatadah and others, that it refers to all the stars in the sky, expressed by the name of the genus. This is the most apparent of the opinions, because it corresponds to the wording in every respect. It is also permissible that "the star" be mentioned in the sense of "the stars."

[Umar] ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

(The most beautiful of the stars in the sky is the Pleiades... and the Pleiades on earth is the adornment of the sky)

Its meaning: the most beautiful of the stars.

As for His words: ﴿when it sets﴾, i.e., when it sinks and disappears. This is if we take it to mean the well-known star. But if we take it to mean the stars of the Qur'an, then its meaning is: when it descends, i.e., when Gabriel (peace be upon him) descends.

It is reported from some that he said: ﴿By the star when it sets﴾ means: when they fall on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., the stars, and this has the same meaning as His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when the stars are scattered﴾, i.e., dispersed. And from some: ﴿when it sets﴾ means its swooping in pursuit of the devils, which is the hurling of meteors, as the Qur'an mentions in many places.

The Words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾ — the first verse came in the form of an oath, and its meaning is: "By the Lord of the star."

His words ﴿Your companion has not strayed﴾ — it is upon this that the oath falls. The Quraysh used to say that Muhammad (ﷺ) was astray and misguided, so Allah the Exalted swore that he had not strayed and had not erred, i.e., he did not miss the [right] way. ﴿Nor has he erred﴾ means he did not depart from rectitude in the matter of his religion and his worldly affairs; al-ghayy (error) is the opposite of rectitude (al-rushd). It is also said: "mā ghawā" means his striving did not fail in what he sought, as though it indicated the existence of what he was seeking.

The poet said:

(Whoever meets good, people praise his affair... and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error)

i.e., whoever's striving fails and does not find what he seeks.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: "bil-hawa" (with desire). Another said: "mā yanṭiqu 'an hawāhu", meaning he does not speak by other than the truth, because whoever follows desire in his speech speaks other than the truth.

And His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a revelation that is revealed﴾. Waḥy (revelation) linguistically means casting something into the self secretly, and in the usage of the people of Islam it is an expression for what God, exalted is He, sends down upon the prophets; and among the prophets is the conveying (of the message) to creation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 5:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾. Most of the people of tafsir (exegesis) hold that what is meant by this is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, and he is the one who taught the Messenger what Allah the Exalted revealed to him.

And Abbad ibn Mansur narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that the words "He has been taught by one mighty in power" refer to Allah the Exalted. Al-quwa (the powers) is the plural of al-quwwah (power). Ibn Abbas said: among the power of Jibril is that he thrust his wing beneath the seventh earth, uprooted the cities of Lot, lifted them up to the sky, and then overturned them. And from Ka'b al-Ahbar: Iblis confronted Jesus, peace be upon him, on one of the mountain passes, and made for him, and Jibril struck him with his wing in a blow that cast him off to India.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 53, verse 6:

Allah's words: ﴿Endowed with strength; so he stood firm﴾. Al-Hasan said: "Endowed with strength" means: endowed with a fine appearance (manzar hasan). Others said, and this is the preferable view: endowed with power (quwwah). It is said: a rope that is mari, meaning firmly twisted (muhkam al-fatl).

As for His words, ﴿so he stood firm﴾, it means: Jibril stood firm on the horizon of the sky in the form in which he was created. This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Alqamah, Qurrah ibn Sharahil, and most of the people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir). It is narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that it refers to Allah, the Exalted, but the sounder view is the first.

**Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 7:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And he is in the highest horizon﴾ refer to the horizon from whose side the sun rises. It is also said: it is the one from which the day comes. The horizon (al-ufuq) means the sides of the sky. It is also said that "in the highest horizon" means: in the sky. And it is related in the reports: "Jibril (peace be upon him) manifested himself to the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form in which he was created, and he had filled the horizon."

And in some narrations: his head was in the sky and his feet were on the earth, for he had filled, with his two wings, what lies between the east and the west.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 8:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then he drew near⁠﴾, meaning: Jibril drew near to the Prophet, peace be upon him.

And His saying: ﴿and descended⁠﴾, meaning: he increased in nearness. Some of them said: His saying, ﴿Then he drew near and descended⁠﴾, is by inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir, transposition of the words' order).

And His saying: ﴿descended⁠﴾, meaning: he swooped down and let himself fall from the sky. Then he drew near, meaning: Jibril drew near to the Prophet, and the distance between them became ﴿two bow-lengths or closer⁠﴾, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So he was two bow-lengths away or nearer⁠﴾, meaning: between them was the measure of two bows or less than that. Qab (قاب) is a Yemeni dialect usage with this meaning. The poet said:

((Do you not know that Rashimah would not have been / To cheat us from beyond a qab of the thumb?))

It is narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that qab is half the thumb. Asbāt narrated from al-Suddi that His saying, ﴿So he was two bow-lengths away or nearer⁠﴾, meaning: the measure of two cubits. Mujahid said: from the bowstring to the grip. It was also said: from the notch to the notch. If it is asked: when you apply this to Jibril, what is the construction of the verse? The answer: its meaning is that when Jibril rose up on the highest horizon in his own form, the Prophet fainted, and this is related in the reports because of the greatness of what he saw. Then Jibril moved from his form to the form in which he used to meet the Prophet, which was the form of a man, and drew near to the Prophet. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then he drew near⁠﴾. Then he lowered his head toward him, in the sense of His saying: ﴿and descended⁠﴾, and embraced him, thus calming him from his terror.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 53, verse 9:

If it is asked: what is the meaning of His words ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾? The word "aw" (or) expresses doubt, and doubt is not permissible for Allah, the Exalted. And if it is taken in the sense of "wa" (and), then it should have said: "So he was at a distance from him of two bow-lengths." Also, why mention the two bows here and single them out for mention, when He could have described it with something else other than the bow and not needed to mention two bows?

The answer: The Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, in the manner in which they addressed one another and understood one another. On this basis the verse was revealed: "Indeed, if you had seen it, you would have said that the nearness between them was two bow-lengths or less." It is also said: "or more or less." As for the mention of the bow, it is in accordance with what they were accustomed to, and the closeness of the bow to the bowstring is well known. It is also said that "two bows" here means one bow, and we have mentioned that a single thing may be referred to with the dual form. The apparent meaning is that the two bows are meant literally, and this is not objectionable in the language of the Arabs, nor is it far-fetched.

The second opinion regarding the verse: that His words ﴿then he drew near﴾ mean that Muhammad drew near to his Lord.

And His words ﴿and he came down﴾ mean that he increased in nearness. In the narration of Malik ibn Sa'sa'a, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "While I was sitting, Jibril came to me and struck me between the shoulders. I stood up, and there was a tree on which were two nests. I sat in one of them, and Jibril sat in the other. We rose up to the sky, and I saw a great light. I looked, and Jibril was like a ḥils (a mat placed under a saddle). I knew the greatness of his fear of God compared with my fear, and the veil was lifted between us." In some narrations he said: "Jibril departed from me, the voices grew still, and I heard from my Lord: 'Draw near, O Muhammad.'" This wording is mentioned in the Sahih, and it refers to Muhammad's drawing near to his Lord on the night of the Mi'raj (Night Journey and Ascension).

The third opinion: that the meaning of His words ﴿then he drew near﴾ is that the Lord drew near to Muhammad. This wording is also established, and it is according to what Allah wills.

And His words ﴿and he came down﴾ mean that He increased in nearness. The opinion known among most scholars is the first, and it is the safest.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 53, verse 10:

The words of God, the Exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: "So Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah what He revealed," and he is Muhammad.

The second view: "So He revealed to His servant what He revealed," meaning: Allah, the Exalted, revealed to Muhammad what He revealed. In the reports it is related that among what Allah revealed to him was that He had prescribed fifty prayers upon this community in the day and night, then it was reduced to five. [And among] what was revealed to him also was the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah. And among what was revealed to him that night was that He forgave his community their grave sins (al-muqhamat) so long as they did not associate partners with Allah. "Meaning: He forgives."

The Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 53, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. The exegetes said: its meaning is: it saw something, and it spoke truly concerning what it reported of its seeing. It is also said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, meaning: the heart saw what it saw in reality, and it was not in imagination and supposition.

The Arabs say: "His eye deceived him (kadhdhabat-hu 'aynuhu)" when something appeared to him in imagination other than its reality.

Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi (the grammarian) said: it is said, "So-and-so did not lie in the hadith (ma kadhdhaba fulan al-hadith)," meaning: he did not lie in it.

It has also been recited as ﴿mā kadhdhaba al-fu'ād mā ra'ā﴾, from the verb of denial (al-takdhib), but the first reading is preferable. The poet said:

"Your two eyes deceived you, or you saw, in the valley-bottom, the darkness of night, from al-Rabab, as a phantom."

It is also said: "the heart did not deny the eye," meaning: it did not make it imagine that it knew something when it had not made it know. It has been established from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Muhammad saw his Lord with his heart twice." If someone says: the believers see Him with their hearts, and that is nothing but knowledge of Him, so what is the meaning of singling out the Prophet? The answer: they said that Allah, may He be exalted, created a sight for his heart, so he saw with his heart as a person sees with his eye. And according to the first view, the seeing is directed to Jibril.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he saw?﴾ That is, will you argue with him? Their disputation was the disputation of doubters and deniers. It is related that they asked him to describe the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, and questioned him about their caravan on the road and how near it was to Makkah.

It is also read as "afatamrūnahu ʿalā mā yarā" (أفتمرونه), meaning: will you deny him? The poet said:

(If you have forsaken a brother of truth and nobility... then you have denied a brother who never used to deny you.) That is, you denied (jaḥadta)."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾, means: he saw Jibril, peace be upon him, in another descent, i.e., another time. If it is said: he had seen him many times, so what is the meaning of "another descent"? The answer: he did not see Jibril in [the form in which he was created] except twice: once at the highest horizon, and that was at the beginning of the revelation. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: that was like a sign which the Prophet was shown, so that he would know that it was from Allah. The second time he saw him was at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (sidrat al-muntaha) on the night of the Ascension (mi'raj), as He said: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary﴾. The sidra is the jujube tree (shajarat al-nabq). In the tafsir it is said that it is in the seventh heaven, and it is said: in the sixth. From ikrimah: it is on the right of the Throne.

It has been established from the Prophet that he said: "The Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary was raised for me, and its fruits are like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root there issue four rivers: two apparent rivers and two hidden rivers," as we have explained.

Opinions differ on the meaning of "the Utmost Boundary" (al-muntaha). Some said: the knowledge of the angels ends at it, and they do not know what lies beyond it, and this is the well-known view.

The second view: whatever ascends to the heaven ends at it, and whatever descends from above ends at it.

In some reports: the angels ascend with the deeds of the children of Adam, until, when they reach the Lote Tree, they are taken from them, and they do not know what lies beyond that.

Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) has transmitted the second view which we have mentioned, traced back to the Prophet.

The third view: the meaning of "the one at which it ends" is that the station of Jibril ends at it. There is another view regarding the verse, namely that the meaning of His saying: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent﴾ is that Muhammad saw his Lord in another descent, and we have mentioned the saying of Ibn Abbas earlier.

The Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah be pleased with them, differed on this. Ibn Mas'ud and a group said: he saw Jibril, and did not see Allah, exalted is He.

From Masruq, who said: A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Whoever claims three things has greatly fabricated a lie against Allah: whoever claims that Muhammad knows what will happen tomorrow has greatly fabricated a lie; Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾, and she mentioned the verse. Whoever claims that Muhammad concealed any of the revelation has greatly fabricated a lie; Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾. And whoever claims that Muhammad saw his Lord has greatly fabricated a lie; Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him﴾, the verse."

Ikrimah narrated from Ibn Abbas: "That Muhammad saw his Lord on the night of the Ascension with his own eyes." This is the view of Anas, Ka'b al-Ahbar, and a great many of the Successors, among them al-Hasan and Ikrimah: that Allah divided His vision and His speech between Muhammad and Musa. So Musa was spoken to twice, and Muhammad saw his Lord twice. This is the view of a group of the imams, among them Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishaq, and others. In some narrations: intimate friendship (khullah) was given to Ibrahim, speech to Musa, and vision to Muhammad.

If it is said: how is it permissible for Allah to be seen in this world? The answer: he did not see Him in this world; and even if he did in this world, then whatever Allah does and honours one of His prophets with is permissible without asking how.

In a report from Zirr ibn Hubaysh from Ibn Mas'ud regarding the meaning of the verse: "The Prophet saw Jibril, and he had six hundred wings." The report is sound. It has been established, by the narration of Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet said: "I saw my Lord in the most beautiful form." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 15:

And His saying: ﴿Near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾, meaning: the believers take refuge in it on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it. And it has been said: the angels take refuge in it.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "Like crows that alight upon the trees." In the verse there is evidence that the Garden is in the heavens and that it is created, and whoever claims that it is not created is a disbeliever by this verse.

And from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: "Jannat al-Ma'wa is the Garden of lodging." And from some of them: "The Garden of abode and station." And from some of them: "Jibril and the angels brought near (al-muqarrabun) take refuge in it."

Ka'b al-Ahbar said: "It is a garden in which there are green birds, within whose crops are the spirits of the martyrs."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 16:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿When there covered the lote-tree that which covered﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: it is covered by a swarm of golden moths (farash min dhahab). And from al-Hasan: it is covered by the light of the Lord, exalted is He. In some traditions: the angels asked permission from their Lord to look at Muhammad on the night of the Mi'raj (the Ascension), so He permitted them, and they gathered upon the lote-tree.

In this hadith, the Prophet said: "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying Allah, exalted is He." Abu al-Hasan Ibn Faris related it and said: this is the meaning of His statement: ﴿When there covered the lote-tree that which covered﴾. In some narrations: it is covered by golden locusts (jarad min dhahab). Know that the lote-tree is a tree that combines three things: far-reaching shade, a delicious taste, and a pleasant fragrance; likewise faith combines three things: intention, speech, and action. Know also that we have mentioned the disagreement of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah be pleased with them, as to whether he saw his Lord on the night of the Mi'raj or not.

Abu al-Husayn Ibn Faris mentioned in his tafsir reports other than those we have mentioned. He related from Ibn 'Umar that Allah, exalted is He, veiled Himself from His creation with light, darkness, and fire. It is also narrated from Abu al-Aliyah al-Riyahi, may Allah have mercy on him, that the Prophet said: "On the night of the Mi'raj I saw a river, and I saw behind it a veil, and I saw behind the veil light, and I do not know what is beyond that." It is also narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that "the Prophet saw his Lord with his heart as one sees with the eye."

In a narration of Abu Dharr: "The Prophet was asked, 'Did you see your Lord?' He said: 'Light, how could I see Him?'" The reports on this matter differ, and Allah knows best the correct position regarding that. It should be said: if the transmission is established that he saw his Lord, we affirm the vision and believe in it; and if the transmission is not established, then the more appropriate position is that he did not see Him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 17:

The words of the Most High: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. In the exegesis it is said that its meaning is: he did not turn to the right or to the left. It is also said that its meaning is: it did not fall short of what he was commanded to look upon, and his sight did not go beyond, in looking, what he was commanded to look at. The meaning of zaygh (swerving) in the language is: inclining with it (al-mayl bihi), and the meaning of tughyan (transgression) is: going beyond (al-tajawuz).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 53, verse 18:

The words of God Most High: ﴿And he certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: That is Jibril (Gabriel), and he has six hundred wings which fill the horizon. In another narration: from his feathers there scatter pearls and rubies (and amulets). In another narration from Ibn Mas'ud: that he saw a green rafraf (silken cushion/canopy) which filled the horizon.

The construction of the verse is: "He saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest sign." And it has been said: he saw of the greatest signs of his Lord, namely the light which he saw on that night.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah (chapter) 53, verses 19–20:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat, al-ʿUzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ Its meaning: Have you considered these idols you worship? Do they possess anything of what God the Exalted has mentioned? Or do they have the loftiness, exaltedness and power that we have described?

As for the explanation of these idols: al-Lat (Allāt) was an idol worshipped by Thaqīf. It is said that it was a rock. As for al-ʿUzza, it was a tree worshipped by Ghaṭafān, Jushm and Sulaym. It is also said that it was a house with custodians (sadana, the keepers of the shrine), and the Arabs would hang a bracelet on it and adorn it with wool and the like. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to demolish al-ʿUzza. He cut down some trees and demolished part of the structure, then returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "Did you see anything?" He said: "No." He said: "You have not done it. Go back." So he went back, exaggerated in the demolition, and killed the custodians. They had been saying: "O ʿUzza, make her blind! O ʿUzza, destroy her!" He said: "A naked woman came out from the inside of al-ʿUzza, her hair loose, calling for woe and destruction and throwing dust on her head. Khālid struck her with the sword and killed her." Then he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him. He said: "That was al-ʿUzza; she will not be worshipped after this day." This is a well-known report.

As for Manat, it was an idol at Qudayd, between Mecca and Medina. It is also said: at al-Mushallal.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: He only said ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ because they believed that Manat was below al-Lat and al-ʿUzza. In the exegesis it is said that al-Lat was a man who used to knead sawīq (a porridge of roasted grain) on a stone, and whoever ate from it would become fat. When he died, they worshipped him and took a stone (in his likeness).

The poet said:

(Do not worship al-Lat, for God will destroy her,
and how can she help you when she cannot help herself?)

Know that we have mentioned in Surah al-Ḥajj that the Prophet recited this surah to the polytheists, and when he reached this verse, Satan cast upon his tongue: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for." This was narrated by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When he recited ([thus]), the polytheists went out and said: 'We only wanted this from you: that you do not criticise our gods or revile them, and that you acknowledge that they have intercession on the Day of Resurrection.' When he reached the end of the surah, the Prophet prostrated, and the Muslims and the polytheists all prostrated together. Then Gabriel came to him and commanded him to recite the surah to him, and he recited it as he had recited it to the polytheists. He said: 'This is not what I revealed to you,' and he exposed that from his recitation. The Prophet was deeply grieved by this, since Satan had done what he had done upon his tongue. So God the Exalted revealed, consoling and comforting him: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire…﴾ [to the end of the verse]. Then, when the Messenger retracted what had been heard from him and returned to reviling their gods and criticising them, the polytheists returned to what they had been upon."

In the story it is also said that this news had reached Abyssinia, that the Muslims and the polytheists had come to agreement, and that the disbelievers had prostrated with the Prophet's prostration, including al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who was their elder and chief. He raised dust to his forehead and prostrated upon it. So the Muslims returned from Abyssinia, but when they had reached part of the way, the news reached them, and they went back to Abyssinia.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah (chapter) 53, verses 19–20:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat, al-ʿUzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ Its meaning: Have you considered these idols you worship? Do they possess anything of what God the Exalted has mentioned? Or do they have the loftiness, exaltedness and power that we have described?

As for the explanation of these idols: al-Lat (Allāt) was an idol worshipped by Thaqīf. It is said that it was a rock. As for al-ʿUzza, it was a tree worshipped by Ghaṭafān, Jushm and Sulaym. It is also said that it was a house with custodians (sadana, the keepers of the shrine), and the Arabs would hang a bracelet on it and adorn it with wool and the like. It has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to demolish al-ʿUzza. He cut down some trees and demolished part of the structure, then returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "Did you see anything?" He said: "No." He said: "You have not done it. Go back." So he went back, exaggerated in the demolition, and killed the custodians. They had been saying: "O ʿUzza, make her blind! O ʿUzza, destroy her!" He said: "A naked woman came out from the inside of al-ʿUzza, her hair loose, calling for woe and destruction and throwing dust on her head. Khālid struck her with the sword and killed her." Then he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned this to him. He said: "That was al-ʿUzza; she will not be worshipped after this day." This is a well-known report.

As for Manat, it was an idol at Qudayd, between Mecca and Medina. It is also said: at al-Mushallal.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: He only said ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ because they believed that Manat was below al-Lat and al-ʿUzza. In the exegesis it is said that al-Lat was a man who used to knead sawīq (a porridge of roasted grain) on a stone, and whoever ate from it would become fat. When he died, they worshipped him and took a stone (in his likeness).

The poet said:

(Do not worship al-Lat, for God will destroy her,
and how can she help you when she cannot help herself?)

Know that we have mentioned in Surah al-Ḥajj that the Prophet recited this surah to the polytheists, and when he reached this verse, Satan cast upon his tongue: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is to be hoped for." This was narrated by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "When he recited ([thus]), the polytheists went out and said: 'We only wanted this from you: that you do not criticise our gods or revile them, and that you acknowledge that they have intercession on the Day of Resurrection.' When he reached the end of the surah, the Prophet prostrated, and the Muslims and the polytheists all prostrated together. Then Gabriel came to him and commanded him to recite the surah to him, and he recited it as he had recited it to the polytheists. He said: 'This is not what I revealed to you,' and he exposed that from his recitation. The Prophet was deeply grieved by this, since Satan had done what he had done upon his tongue. So God the Exalted revealed, consoling and comforting him: ﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire…﴾ [to the end of the verse]. Then, when the Messenger retracted what had been heard from him and returned to reviling their gods and criticising them, the polytheists returned to what they had been upon."

In the story it is also said that this news had reached Abyssinia, that the Muslims and the polytheists had come to agreement, and that the disbelievers had prostrated with the Prophet's prostration, including al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who was their elder and chief. He raised dust to his forehead and prostrated upon it. So the Muslims returned from Abyssinia, but when they had reached part of the way, the news reached them, and they went back to Abyssinia.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ This is said in the manner of rebuke directed at them, because they used to say: "These idols are in the forms of the angels, and the angels are the daughters of Allah." This is the statement of some of them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 22:

And His saying: ﴿That, then, is an unjust division﴾, meaning: unjust (jā'irah). The real meaning is: if you dislike daughters for yourselves, then it is more fitting that you dislike them for God, exalted is He.

The lexicographers (ahl al-lughah) have transmitted this word from the Arabs in four forms: ḍayzā, ḍawzā without a hamza, ḍa'zā, and ḍāzī without a hamza. These dialectal forms are in addition to what was revealed in the Revelation (al-tanzīl).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are nothing but names that you and your fathers have named; God has sent down no authority (sultan) for them.﴾ That is: no proof (hujjah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that every "sultan" in the Qur'an carries the meaning of proof (hujjah).

His saying: ﴿They follow nothing but conjecture (zann).﴾ It is mentioned in some reports that the believer does good deeds and so his opinion of God is good, while the hypocrite does evil deeds and so his opinion is evil. And in some reports: "The most false of speech is conjecture (al-zann)."

His saying: ﴿And what the souls desire.﴾ That is: what the self (nafs) calls to.

His saying: ﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord guidance (al-huda).﴾ That is: the path of rectitude (rushd) and truth (haqq).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 24:

And the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or does man have whatever he wishes?﴾ Its meaning is: "Does man have whatever he wishes?" That is, he does not have what he wishes. Know that wishful longing (al-umniyyah) is blameworthy, while determined will (al-irادah) is praiseworthy. The difference between them is that wishful longing is a desire which is not confirmed by action, whereas determined will is that which is confirmed by action.

And in some reports from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "The intelligent person is one who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, while the foolish person is one who follows his desires and wishes against Allah for forgiveness." And from some of them: "Wishful hopes are the capital of the bankrupt."
"And His saying: ﴿So to Allah belong the Hereafter and the first life﴾ — meaning: sovereignty belongs to Him in the Hereafter and in this world."

The Exalted said: ﴿And how many an angel there is in the heavens﴾. It is narrated from Ka'b al-Ahbar that he said: There is no place the width of a palm (shibr) in the sky except that there is an angel in it, standing or prostrating.

Something similar has also been narrated concerning the earth from others. And "kam" (how many) in the language is for expressing multiplicity.

As for His saying: ﴿Their intercession will avail nothing, except after Allah gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾, the meaning is: they do not possess intercession for anyone until Allah grants permission for it and approves of it. In some tafsirs it is stated that this is a response to the claim of the polytheists that "the exalted cranes (al-gharaniq) intercede with Allah on the Day of Resurrection," and these are the idols. So Allah the Exalted informed that no one possesses intercession except by the permission of Allah the Exalted and His approval in that.

Almighty God's words: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels with the names of females﴾. This is their saying about the idols, and their naming of them al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat, the names of females. They used to say: these idols are in the form of the angels.
And His saying: ﴿And they have no knowledge of it. They follow only conjecture, and indeed conjecture avails nothing against the truth at all.﴾ That is: it never stands in for the truth, ever.

Almighty God says: ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance and desires nothing but the worldly life.﴾ It is said that this verse was revealed before the revelation of the verse of the sword, and then the verse of the sword abrogated it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 30:

And His saying: ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾, meaning: they know only the matter of livelihood in the life of this world. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri, who said: "How many a man there is who taps a dirham with his fingernail and they describe it, and he makes no mistake about it, yet he does not know how to pray."

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of who is guided﴾, meaning: He knows the guided and the misguided, the believer and the disbeliever, and nothing of their affairs is hidden from Him.

And His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, that He may recompense those who did evil with what they have done and recompense those who did good with the best [reward]﴾ — i.e., with Paradise.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 32:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir) of wrongdoing and the abominations﴾. It was also read as "kabir al-ithm" (the singular). We have already explained the meaning of al-kaba'ir earlier. It has been said: it is everything for which Allah has threatened the Fire. And al-fawahish: the acts of disobedience.

His saying: ﴿except for the lapses (al-lamam)﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it is that a person commits a sin and then repents of it, that is, he does it once and does not persist in it. And also from him, he said: "I have not seen anything more resembling al-lamam than what Abu Hurayrah narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed Allah the Exalted has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eye is looking, the adultery of the hand is touching, the soul desires and longs, and the private part either confirms that or denies it.'" And this is a sound hadith.

According to this view, al-lamam is looking, touching, and what is similar to that. In this regard there is the hadith of Nabhan al-Tammar, which we mentioned in Surah Hud.

In the verse there is a third view: that al-lamam is the minor sins (al-saghair). And there is a fourth view: that al-lamam is what the Muslims did in the Jahiliyyah before their Islam; when they embraced Islam, pardon was granted for them.

It has also been said: al-lamam is glancing suddenly, then immediately lowering one's gaze. And from some of them:

(If You forgive, O Allah, then forgive much, / for which of Your servants is not a sinner.)

Some have transmitted this with a chain traced back to the Prophet. As for the meaning of "illa" (except) in the verse, some said it is disjunctive (munqati'), as if he said: "but the lamam." Others said the exception is in its literal sense, and al-lamam are abominations, except that Allah the Exalted pardons them by His will.

His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is of vast forgiveness﴾, that is, abundant in forgiveness.

His saying: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾, its meaning: He began your creation from dust, then from a drop of semen.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers﴾, meaning: He was knowing of your conditions while you were fetuses in the wombs of the mothers, ignorant of your own conditions.

His saying: ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾, that is: do not praise yourselves.

His saying: ﴿He knows best who is righteous﴾, that is: He knows best those who are God-fearing. From 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: al-lamam is that a person resolves upon a sin and then does not commit it. This was mentioned by al-Qaffal al-Shashi in his tafsir. And it is related from Abu Hurayrah that he said: al-lamam is the squeeze and the kiss.

As for His saying: ﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾, we have already explained it. In the tafsir of al-Naqqash: a man from the Jews, whenever a child of his died, would say: "He is a righteous one (siddiq)." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse as a refutation of them. It is also said: the verse concerns a man who reports his fasting, his prayer, and his good deeds among people, and some of them would say: "We did such-and-such, and we did such-and-such." So Allah the Exalted forbade them from that. Know that a man praising himself is disliked, and likewise a man praising another to his face.

In the well-known report: a man praised another man in the presence of the Prophet, and he said: "Woe to you, you have cut off the neck of your brother. If one of you must say something, let him say: 'I think so-and-so is such,' and I do not declare anyone pure before Allah."

In another report: "Throw dust in the faces of the flatterers," narrated by al-Miqdad from the Prophet.

His saying: ﴿He knows best who is righteous﴾ has already been explained.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾ That is, he turned away from faith in Allah.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 34:

And His saying: ﴿And gave a little and withheld﴾. The meaning of His saying "akda" (withheld): that is, he cut off his giving.

It is also said: "akda" means "ajbal" (reached a rock). From this comes al-kudya (the hard rock), which is when a man digs a well and reaches a place where he cannot work because of rock or something similar; this is called al-kudya. The meaning of His saying "ajbal" is: he reached a mountain (jabal). In the exegesis it is related that the verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and it is also said concerning al-As ibn Wa'il. He used to attend the gathering of the Prophet (ﷺ) and listen to the Qur'an. Then the polytheists reproached him, and he said: "I fear the punishment." One of them said to him: "Give me something and I will bear your punishment on the Day of Resurrection." So he gave him something, and he (the other) took it upon himself on his behalf. Accordingly, His saying "gave a little" means: he listened and inclined toward Islam.

As for His saying "akda" (withheld), it means: he cut off what he had given. Muqatil said: he gave with his tongue and cut off with his heart. Some transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning of the verse is: he obeyed and then disobeyed. Some mentioned that a man from the ignorant Bedouins, who had embraced Islam and came to Madina, began saying: "Who will buy my good deeds for a sa' of dates?" Abu Khaythama al-Ansari, who was a man of goodness, said: "I will buy them from you for a wasq of dates." The wasq is sixty sa'. So the Bedouin sold him his good deeds and took the wasq, and God Most High revealed this verse concerning the Bedouin. The well-known view is the first opinion.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 35:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ That is: he knows. Seeing (al-ru'yah) may mean sight with the eye, and it may mean knowledge. The Arabs say: "I saw so-and-so a scholar," meaning: "I knew." The meaning of the verse is: Does the one who bears the sins on behalf of al-Walid have knowledge of the unseen, so that he knows that he will bear them for him on the Day of Resurrection?

Almost all of this passage is a tafsir commentary, so I'll translate it as it stands.

God's words: ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Moses?﴾ Its meaning: "Has he not been told?"

As for His words, ﴿what is in the scriptures of Moses﴾, Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned that God sent down one hundred [and four] books: thirty scrolls (ṣaḥīfa) upon Sheth, fifty upon Idris, twenty upon Abraham, and four upon Moses, David, Jesus, and Muhammad, peace be upon them all.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 37:

His words: ﴿And Ibrahim, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri recited "wafa" (وفى) with a light (unshaddahed) fa', meaning: he carried out what he was commanded. It is also said: "He fulfilled [the command] concerning the sacrifice of his son."

As for the recitation that is well known with the shadda (tashdid), it is permissible that it carries the meaning of "wafa", except that it is emphasized by the shadda. It is also said: he fulfilled [the thirty shares of] Islam. Al-Hasan said: "He was never commanded with a matter except that he acted upon it."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Islam has thirty shares (sahm), and none fulfilled all of them except Ibrahim and Muhammad, peace be upon them both." Al-Farra' said: the meaning of "wafa" is: he reached [the end]. And it is narrated from al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil who said: "Between Nuh and Ibrahim there were generations who would seize the neighbour for the sin of the neighbour, the paternal cousin for the sin of the paternal cousin, and the close friend for the sin of the close friend. Then Ibrahim came and conveyed [the message] from Allah, the Exalted."

Translation:

"Let no bearer of burdens bear the burden of another" (Q. 53:38). That is: no one is taken to account for the sin of another.
Qur'an 53:39 (﴿And that there is not for man except what he strives for﴾). Its meaning: if he strives toward good, he will meet good; and if he strives toward evil, he will meet evil.

And His saying: ﴿And that his effort will be seen﴾ — meaning: he will see it, in the sense that God, exalted is He, will show him it, namely the recompense with which He will repay him for it, and this is the meaning

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 41:

His saying: ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾, meaning: the most perfect and complete.

The Lord's words, "And that to your Lord is the final end" (Q. 53:42): that is, the return of the servants and their coming back to Him. Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Baqir said: "The intellects wander about in it," meaning they become bewildered. According to this, the meaning of the verse is that when intellects reach His attributes they become bewildered, meaning that they cannot grasp His attributes in their completeness. In some tafsirs it is said that one of the angels reflected upon Allah, the Exalted, and a cry was cried out at him, so his intellect wandered, and so he is called among the angels "the one who has wandered."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 43:

His the Exalted's saying: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He makes the people of Paradise laugh, and makes the people of the Fire weep. It is also said: He makes laugh with the promise, and makes weep with the threat. It is also said: He makes the earth laugh with vegetation, and makes the sky weep with rain. The most correct of the sayings is that He makes creation laugh and makes them weep.

Almighty Allah's words: ﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾. It is said: He causes the fathers to die, and gives life to the sons. It is also said: He causes some people to die through misguidance, and gives life through guidance. The more correct view is that He causes creation to die and gives them life.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He created the pair, the male and the female﴾, meaning: the two kinds. Al-Dahhak said: Adam and Eve. The more sound view is that it refers to male and female among the children of Adam.

"And His saying: ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾ — meaning: when it is measured out (tuqaddar). The Arabs say: "Mā tamanná tilka [al-amānī]," meaning: that measurer measured that. And it has been said: "when it is emitted" is an expression for intercourse, meaning: from a drop of semen that comes about through copulation."

Almighty Allah says: ﴿And that it is He who originates the second creation﴾. That is, the resurrection on the Day of Judgment. He said "the second" (al-ukhra) because it is the second after the first creation (al-nash'ah al-ula), and the first creation is the beginning of creation.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who makes rich and gives property﴾. Its meaning: He gives and widens. So His saying ﴿aqnā﴾ means: He gives qinya (property held as capital). Qinya is the original wealth that is acquired. They said: it is like camels, cattle, estates, crops and the like. It is also said: He makes rich (aghnā) with gold and silver, and gives property (aqnā) with other than them of wealth. It is also said: aghnā and aqnā mean: He gives, and makes content with what He has given. Al-Qutaybi said: aghnā means: He gives wealth; and afnā means: He gives servants, as if He gave him someone to serve him. And he said: aghnā means: He gives with what He gives. It is reported from some of them: aghnā means: He makes himself rich, as if He described Himself as self-sufficient. And His saying ﴿aqnā﴾ means: He made His creatures most in need of Himself. It is also said: aghnā and aqnā mean: He widened and restricted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 49:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And that He is the Lord of Sirius﴾. In the exegesis (tafsir): there was a man from Khuza'ah who deviated from the religion of his forefathers and worshipped al-Sha'ra al-'Abur (al-Shi'ra al-'Abur, Sirius, the "Crossing" Sirius). It is a star behind al-Jawza' (Orion), called al-Mirzam, and the two Sha'ris are: the first (ihdahuma) is al-Ghumaysa', and the other is al-'Abur. Al-Ghumaysa' is in the Milky Way, and al-'Abur is behind al-Jawza', and it is called the Dog of al-Jawza'. That man used to worship al-Sha'ra, and he would say: "It crosses the sphere transversely, unlike the other stars, for it crosses the sands." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse, and mentioned that He is the Creator of the Sha'ra that you worship. This was related by Mujahid, Qatadah and others. And it is related from some of them that it is Venus (al-Zuhara), but this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse.

"The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿĀd﴾. If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "the first ʿĀd", when ʿĀd was one and not two? The answer: ʿĀd and Thamūd were both from the offspring of Ādam, son of Sām, son of Nūḥ. ʿĀd are the people of Hūd, and they are the first ʿĀd; and Thamūd are the people of Ṣāliḥ, and they are the other ʿĀd."
And His saying: ﴿And Thamud — He spared none of them﴾. That is, He destroyed them and annihilated them.

It is said in the commentary on the verse: ﴿And the people of Noah before them. Indeed they were more unjust and more transgressing.﴾ That is, they were greater in wrongdoing and more intense in rebellion.

In the narrative (al-qissa): a man among them would bring his son to Noah and say, "Beware of this old man, and be careful lest he lead you astray. My father brought me to him when I was at your age, and he warned me against him just as I am warning you against him."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 53, verse 53:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And the overturned cities He cast down⦆ (al-mu'tafikah ahwa). Al-Mu'tafikah are the cities of Lut (Lot), which were overturned by the earth with them, meaning: they were turned upside down with them.

As for His words ﴿ahwa﴾ (cast down): it is said "hawa" (hawa) when something falls, and "ahwa" (ahwa) when one causes it to fall. We have already explained that Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, uprooted them from their foundation and carried them up to the lowest heaven, until the people of the lowest heaven heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of their roosters. There were four hundred thousand men in them, and it has been said that they were more than that. Then Jibril overturned them, and they came down falling, and this is the meaning of His words: ﴿And the overturned cities He cast down﴾. Ikrimah said: they continue to shake and sink within the earth until the Hour is established. The Arabs say "ahwa," meaning he fell into a pit, and al-hawah is the hole (al-huffah).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 54:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So there covered them that which covered﴾. That is: there covered them, of the stones, that which covered. It is said: "[There covered them] of the punishment of Allah that which covered." Al-taghshiyah (the covering) is al-taghtiyah (the covering over).

In the narrative: the stone would follow their fleeing until it destroyed them all. There was among them a man in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and a stone stopped for him in the air for seven months. Then he went out, and when he came out and took one step, the stone fell upon him and destroyed him. His name was Abu Righal.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ That is, "will you doubt," meaning "will you be in doubt." It was also said: "will you deny." Al-mira (doubt) linguistically means shakk (doubt). The address is to the disbeliever, meaning: "So which of the bounties of your Lord will you dispute, O disbeliever?"

This is a translation task for a short passage of tafsir, so I'll render it faithfully.

"And His words: ﴿This is a warner of the warners of old﴾ — meaning: a prophet resembling the earlier prophets."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verses 57–58:

And His saying: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near. None besides Allah can reveal it.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "kashifah" (revealing), and why was the feminine ta' (ha') added? The answer: some of them said it is for conformity with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat). Others said its meaning is: "None besides Allah has a soul (nafs) that reveals it," and this is better. The meaning of the verse is that no one knows its knowledge except Allah the Exalted. This is the knowledge of its establishment and its manifestation. It is also said: no one brings it except Allah the Exalted.

It is said: "kashafa 'an al-shay'" means when he made it manifest, i.e., none uncovers the Resurrection or makes it manifest except Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verses 57–58:

And His saying: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near. None besides Allah can reveal it.﴾ If it is asked: what is the meaning of His saying "kashifah" (revealing), and why was the feminine ta' (ha') added? The answer: some of them said it is for conformity with the endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayat). Others said its meaning is: "None besides Allah has a soul (nafs) that reveals it," and this is better. The meaning of the verse is that no one knows its knowledge except Allah the Exalted. This is the knowledge of its establishment and its manifestation. It is also said: no one brings it except Allah the Exalted.

It is said: "kashafa 'an al-shay'" means when he made it manifest, i.e., none uncovers the Resurrection or makes it manifest except Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 59:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse?﴾ That is, the Qur'an.

As for His words ﴿marvel﴾, that is, you wonder at it (tata'ajjabun). Their wonder was that they said: "How has it been sent down to a single man like us?" It is also said: their wonder was at His statement that God is One, as He said elsewhere: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a strange thing!﴾

And His words: ﴿And you laugh and do not weep﴾ mean: it is your duty to weep, not to laugh. In the exegesis (tafsir) it is related: "When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) was not seen laughing until he left this world, except that he would smile." And in some reports: "I am astonished at one who laughs with his mouth full while death is seeking him."

And His saying: ﴿while you are indulging in vanity﴾ — meaning: heedless and unmindful. It is also said: proud and arrogant. Mujahid said: "al-sumud" is singing in the language of Himyar. They say: "O slave-girl, sing (samidi) for us," meaning: sing. It is also called "al-barṭama." Some of them recited:

"The vicissitudes of time struck the women of the family of Harb with a calamity, a sumdan that brought them sumud (singing and lamentation),"

and it is narrated:

"By a measure (of time) that sumdan made for them sumud..."

"He turned their black hair white, and turned their white faces black."

"And His words: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾. Some have taken this to refer to the five daily prayers. It was also said: the verse was revealed in Mecca before the five daily prayers were made obligatory, and the surah is Meccan. According to this, its meaning is: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship [Him]﴾, i.e., submit to Allah and affirm His oneness. It is also said: what is meant is the basic prostration, and what is meant by worship is obedience. This is a place of prostration according to most jurists, except Malik, who said: there is no prostration at all in the mufassal (the final short surahs of the Qur'an). It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ, through the narration of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), that "he (ﷺ) recited Surah al-Najm and prostrated in it, and no one among the people remained except that he prostrated, except for one man who took a pebble and placed it on his forehead, and said: 'This is enough for me.' Abdullah said: 'I saw him later killed as a disbeliever.'" And Allah knows best.
